title: The History of MREs: How Science Replaced the Campfire Cook
fullText: In 1812, an army of roughly 600,000 men marched into Russia behind Napoleon Bonapart. Fewer than 100,000 marched back out. Not all of them fell to Russian musketss. Most of them starved. Soldiers boiled their own leather belts for broth. Cavalry men slit open the veins of their horses to drink the blood, then ate the horses, too, hooves and all. Men froze to death, sitting upright around fires they were too weak to feed. Historians still argue over the exact death toll, but the low estimates put French and Allied losses at around 380,000 men, and disease and starvation killed far more of them than combat ever did. And here is the detail that makes this strange. Napoleon himself had already tried to fix this problem 17 years earlier with a cash prize and a promise. He knew the danger. He knew an army that cannot eat is an army that cannot fight. But there is one cause of the disaster in Russia that rarely makes the textbook. Not the cold, not the cussics. Logistics. Nobody had yet figured out how to keep food edible, portable, and safe to eat hundreds of miles from a kitchen. That problem killed more soldiers across human history than almost any weapon ever built. And today, that exact problem has a solution you can buy on Amazon for about $12, sitting in a plastic pouch in your pantry, shelf stable for years, ready to eat cold out of the bag if you have to. So, how did feeding an army in the field go from 600,000 men starving in the Russian snow to a foil pouch you can heat with a splash of salt water in 10 minutes? This story does not start in Russia. It starts almost 4,000 years earlier on the grasslands of North America, long before anyone had a word for calories or bacteria or shelf life. The people who first solved portable nutrition were not scientists in a laboratory. They were the indigenous nations of the North American plains and the food they invented is called pemkin, a word borrowed from the Cree language from pimikin meaning fat. The process was simple in description and brilliant in execution. Lean meat, usually bison, was cut into thin strips and dried either in the sun or over a low smoky fire until it lost most of its moisture and became nearly immune to spoilage. Then it was pounded into a coarse powder and mixed with rendered fat, sometimes with dried berries added for flavor and a small nutritional boost. The result was dense, greasy, almost indestructible, and absurdly calorie rich. A single pound of pemkin could carry more usable energy than several pounds of fresh meat without refrigeration, without salt, and without spoiling for months or even years if it was kept dry. They did not know the word desiccation. They did not know the word oxidation. They were controlling both anyway through pure trial and observation passed down for generations. This was not a snack. It was survival technology. And it eventually became so valuable that European fur traders in Canada built entire supply chains around buying it from indigenous producers because pemkin, not flour or salted pork, was what actually kept fur trade brigades alive on multi-month journeys through the interior of the continent. Think about that for a second. A recipe developed on the plains of what is now Canada and the northern United States ended up feeding a continent spanning commercial empire. There is a colorful legend attached to Pemkin's origins. The idea that a single unnamed hunter accidentally discovered the technique after leaving strips of meat too close to a rendering pot of fat during a hard winter. That version makes for a nice campfire story, but there is no solid historical record naming any single inventor. And the truth is almost certainly less cinematic. A slow accumulation of practical knowledge refined across countless winters by countless different hands. Still, the fact that a founding myth exists at all tells you something about how valuable this food eventually became. Nobody invents an origin story for something nobody cared about. Halfway around the world, a very different group of people arrived at a strikingly similar answer. Mongol cavalry under Genghask Khan in the 1200s moved across Asia at a speed no other army of the era could match and part of the reason was food. Mongol riders carried dried curds of milk called karut which could be dissolved in water or simply chewed on the move along with strips of dried and salted meat. There is a persistent legend that Mongol horsemen tenderized raw meat by placing it under their saddles while riding. That story is almost certainly exaggerated, if not invented outright, by outside observers trying to explain Mongol endurance in the most dramatic terms possible. But the underlying truth beneath the legend is real. Mongol logistics depended on food that required no fire, no cooking pot, and no supply wagon. No fire, no smoke, no delay. An army that does not need to stop and cook is an army that can outrun everyone who does. The Mongols understood that principle centuries before anyone wrote it down as military doctrine. The Roman legions centuries earlier still had already been wrestling with the exact same puzzle. A Roman soldier on campaign carried a ration called busilatum, a twicebaked hard biscuit similar to what later armies would call hardtac along with pusca, a mixture of vinegar and water that was cheap, mildly antiseptic, and better for morale than it sounds. Rome also depended on salted pork, dried grain, and cheese. Foods chosen specifically because they traveled well and did not require daily preparation. This was not about seasoning food for pleasure. This was about a logistical machine. Rome built roads in part to move armies in the food that fed them. And a Roman army that could feed itself efficiently could stay in the field far longer than an enemy that could not. salt, grain, vinegar, dried meat. [music] Three ordinary ingredients doing the extraordinary work of keeping the largest fighting force in the ancient world alive, marching, and lethal. Roman commanders understood something that modern military planners still teach in staff colleges today, essentially unchanged, roughly 2,000 years later, that logistics wins wars long before strategy or courage ever get the chance to. This is where the story starts to repeat itself again and again across every empire that ever tried to project power beyond its own borders. Rome could conquer only as far as its supply lines could reach. So could Napoleon, so eventually could the United States. For roughly 2,000 years after Rome, the underlying technology barely changed. Armies and navies survived on salted meat packed in barrels, hard biscuit that could crack a tooth, and dried fish, none of which lasted forever, and all of which degraded badly over long voyages or long campaigns. This was the era of the great age of sail, and it came with a body count that modern soldiers would find almost unimaginable. Sailors on long ocean voyages routinely died of scurvy, a disease caused by vitamin C deficiency that rots the gums, reopens old wounds, and eventually kills. Historians estimate that scurvy killed more sailors during the age of sail than combat, storms, and shipwreck combined with death tolls in the hundreds of thousands across the centuries of European naval expansion. James Lind, a Scottish naval surgeon, ran one of the first controlled clinical trials in medical history in 1747 and demonstrated that citrus fruit prevented and cured scurvy. And here is the uncomfortable reality that naval bureaucracies spent decades trying to avoid dealing with. The British Royal Navy did not officially adopt citrus rations for nearly 50 years after Lynn's results were published. Bureaucratic inertia, cost concerns, and simple stubbornness cost thousands of additional lives. In the meantime, the solution existed. Nobody in power wanted to pay for it yet. It was not a mystery. It was not a lack of evidence. It was paperwork, budgets, and institutional stubbornness. quietly costing thousands of lives a year while the fix sat written down in a published medical report gathering dust in an office somewhere in London. That pattern, a workable fix arriving decades before anyone with authority chooses to implement it, will come up again in this story more than once. Meanwhile, back in continental Europe, a different kind of catastrophe was building, one that would finally force the issue. This is where Napoleon re-enters the story. this time as the man who tried seriously and expensively to solve the problem his own army would later die from. In 1795, the French Directory, the government running France before Napoleon consolidated power, offered a reward of 12,000 Franks, worth roughly $300,000 in today's money, to anyone who could invent a reliable method for preserving large quantities of food for French troops on campaign. This was not charity. It was survival math for the state itself. An army that starves cannot conquer and France in the 1790s intended to conquer quite a lot. The man who eventually claimed the prize was Nicholas Apair, a Parisian confectioner, pickler, brewer, and chef with essentially no formal scientific education. For roughly 14 years, Apair experimented largely through pure trial and error, sealing food inside glass jars, corking them, and then submerging them in boiling water for varying lengths of time depending on the food inside. He did not know why it worked. He believed incorrectly that keeping air away from food was the key to preventing spoilage. The actual explanation that heat kills the microorganisms responsible for decay would not be demonstrated until Louis Pastor's work decades later in the 1860s. Apair was in effect running a sterilization process with zero understanding of germ theory using nothing but patience and repetition. And here is the twist. It worked anyway. In 1804, Apair opened what is generally considered the first canning factory in the world in the town of Massie south of Paris. And by 1809, he had preserved a range of foods well enough and documented his method thoroughly enough that the French government awarded him the full 12,000 franc prize. He published his findings the following year in a book whose title translates roughly to the art of preserving all kinds of animal and vegetable substances for several years. Not a modest title, but an accurate one. Shortly afterward, a British merchant named Peter Duran took the concept and adapted it, patenting a version that used 10plated iron canisters instead of fragile glass jars. The 10 can, the ancestor of every can of soup sitting in a modern pantry, was born directly out of a French military food preservation contest. Whether every detail of Apair's 14-year journey has survived accurately across two centuries of retelling remains debated among food historians, but the outcome is not in dispute. The problem that had haunted armies since Rome, keeping food edible over time and distance, finally had a real repeatable, scalable answer. There is a bitter irony sitting right at the center of this breakthrough, though. Apair won his prize in 1809. Napoleon's Grand Arme marched into Russia in 1812, 3 years later, and still starved by the hundreds of thousands. The technology existed. The industrial capacity, the transport infrastructure, and the sheer logistical scale required to can enough food for 600,000 marching men did not exist yet. Not even close. A solution being invented and a solution being deployed at scale turned out to be two entirely different problems separated by decades, sometimes by generations. That gap between invention and implementation is in many ways the real subject of this entire video. The 19th century that followed was a slow uneven scramble to close that gap. American caneries opened within just a few years of Duran's patent. The very first widely credited to Robert Ayes in 1812. Can openers strangely took much longer to catch up because the earliest tin cans were thick and heavy and were originally meant to be hacked open with a hammer and chisel. The dedicated can opener was not patented in the United States until 1858 by Ezra Warner nearly 50 years after the can itself existed. Think about that. Soldiers, sailors, and settlers were eating out of tin cans for close to half a century using whatever sharp object they happen to have on hand. Because the convenience tool everyone assumes came first, actually came almost last. Canned rations saw real, if imperfect, use in later conflicts, including the American Civil War. But the results exposed just how far military food science still had to go. And this is where the story turns dark for a moment because the Civil War is where inadequate food logistics stopped being an inconvenience and became a mass casualty event on both sides of the conflict. Union and Confederate soldiers alike depended heavily on hardtac, a flower and water biscuit baked so hard that soldiers nicknamed it worm castles, sheet iron crackers, and teeth dullers because the biscuits were frequently infested with weevils and maggots that soldiers had to knock out before eating or simply ate along with everything else in the dark. Salted pork, when it was available at all, was often rancid by the time it reached the front. Clean water was scarce. Sanitation in army camps was almost non-existent. The results were catastrophic. Of the roughly 620,000 soldiers who died during the American Civil War, historians estimate that around 2/3 died of disease rather than combat wounds driven overwhelmingly by dysentery, typhoid, and other illnesses tied directly to contaminated food and water and inadequate nutrition. 2/3. Read that again. More American soldiers were killed by their own supply chain indirectly than were killed by enemy bullets and artillery combined. This was not a footnote to the war. This was one of its defining deadliest features and it happened on American soil less than a century after aair had already proven that food could be preserved safely if the process was done correctly and at scale. The knowledge existed. The industrial and logistical machinery to apply it to an army of over two million men across four years of continuous war did not. If you are finding this interesting so far, go ahead and hit subscribe now. This channel covers stories exactly like this one every single week, tracing the hidden histories behind the objects sitting in your own kitchen. And you will not want to miss what is coming because the next stretch of the story is where military food finally stops being a slowmoving disaster and starts becoming an actual applied science. The turning point came with the two World Wars and it came fast. World War I accelerated food canning and preservation technology across every major industrial power as governments realized that feeding millions of mobilized men required industrial thinking, not improvisation. But the real leap, the one that most directly built the road to the modern MRE, happened during World War II. And it happened because of one very specific physiologist with a very specific assignment. In 1941, the United States War Department tasked Anel Keys, a physiologist at the University of Minnesota, with designing a compact, non-p perishable, ready to eat ration that could fit inside a soldier's pocket intended specifically for paratroopers and other highly mobile troops who could not carry bulky field kitchens with them. Keys did not start in a laboratory. He started at a local supermarket, buying hard biscuits, dry sausage, hard candy, and chocolate bars. Essentially building a prototype combat meal out of cheap, dense, shelf stable civilian groceries. His first version weighed roughly 28 ounces and packed around 3,200 calories. This was not about gourmet food, survival, portability, and calories in that order. By May of 1942, the Army placed its first order for 1 million units of what became known as the Kration. The letter K chosen according to most accounts simply because it sounded phonetically distinct from the existing A, B, C, and D rations already in use, not because it stood for keys, though the coincidence stuck in public memory. Anyway, the Kration split each day into three separately boxed meals: breakfast, lunch, and supper. delivering somewhere around 2,800 to 3,000 calories total. Later boxes colorcoded for easy identification in the field. It came packed with canned meat or cheese, [music] dense biscuits, hard candy, powdered coffee or bullion, chewing gum, and even cigarettes. Because 1940s military nutrition science had not yet caught up with what we now know about tobacco. By 1944, over 100 million Krations had been produced. Soldiers being soldiers immediately started complaining, and their complaints were not unreasonable. The Kration was designed for short duration use, recommended for a maximum of around 15 consecutive meals before switching to fuller field rations. But supply chain realities meant many soldiers ate nothing else for weeks at a time. It was monotonous. It was calorically insufficient for men doing sustained heavy combat labor. And it left soldiers with real vitamin deficiencies during extended campaigns. The technology had improved by an order of magnitude compared to hardtack and rancid salt pork. It was not yet actually good. Alongside the Kration ran the C ration, a heavier canned pre-cooked meal first adopted in 1938 and used by American forces clear through the Vietnam War decades later. and the D-ration, an emergency chocolate bar deliberately engineered to be nearly inedible, formulated to withstand temperatures up to about 120° Fahrenheit without melting, and intentionally made unpleasant enough that soldiers would not casually snack on their emergency reserves and burn through them before an actual emergency. Soldiers were instructed to eat it slowly, over roughly half an hour, or dissolve it in boiling water. It worked exactly as designed. Nobody liked it and that was the entire point. By the end of World War II, the underlying science of preserving, packaging, and distributing food to millions of mobile combat troops had advanced further in about 5 years than it had in the previous 2000. But the packaging itself, heavy tin cans, bulky cardboard boxes, was still fundamentally the same 19th century technology a pair had pioneered, just manufactured at an industrial scale he never could have imagined. The next revolution was not going to come from changing what was inside the ration. It was going to come from changing the container itself. And that revolution took root, appropriately enough, in a research laboratory that most Americans have never heard of, tucked into a small town in Massachusetts. Research and development on what would eventually become the modern meal ready to eat, began as early as 1959, much of it conducted at the United States Army NATIC Research and Development Laboratories, later renamed the NATIC Soldier System Center outside Boston. And here is a detail that tends to catch people off guard. A significant portion of this early food science work was not purely military at all. NATIC researchers were simultaneously developing food systems for NASA's early man space flight program in the 1960s. Meaning some of the exact same lightweight preservation and packaging breakthroughs that eventually fed American astronauts orbiting the Earth were engineered by the same labs, sometimes by the same scientists, working just a few buildings apart from the teams designing rations for infantry soldiers. Space food and combat food developed side by side for two groups of people who both needed calories that weighed almost nothing and would not spoil in extreme conditions. By 1963, the Department of Defense had formally launched a coordinated project to design a new generation of ration that could replace the aging heavy can dependent cration. Researchers at NATIC spent years working on the core problem. How to preserve food without the weight, bulk, and slow heat transfer of a metal can. In 1968, food scientists at NATIC working under this program produced what is generally credited as the first true prototype of what would later be called a meal ready to eat. Pairing traditional food preparation techniques with new lightweight packaging designed specifically to replace the canned entre still weighing soldiers down. This was the halfway point of the journey. The concept existed. The packaging that would make it truly practical did not. Not yet. That packaging finally arrived in the mid 1970s and it is arguably the single most important, least glamorous invention in this entire story. It is called the retort pouch. a flexible multi-layer laminate of plastic and thin metal foil that can be filled with food, sealed, and then processed at high temperature and pressure to achieve what food scientists call commercial sterility. Essentially the same sterilization outcome as old-fashioned canning, but inside a container that weighs a fraction as much and takes a fraction of the time to heat through. Work on the retort pouch began around 1975. And because the packaging is thin and flat rather than a thick metal cylinder, heat penetrates it far more quickly and evenly during sterilization, which also happens to preserve flavor and texture noticeably better than old style canning ever could. This was not just a packaging swap. It was not just a lighter can. It was an entirely new relationship between food, heat, and time. NADC's own estimates put the weight reduction versus equivalent canned rations at somewhere around 75%. 3/4 of the weight gone with the food inside lasting under proper storage conditions for years rather than months. The United States military began distributing rations in retort pouches starting in 1978. And the modern MRE program moved into full-scale production between 1980 and 1981 with the very first official MRE menus dated to 1981. Field testing followed over the next several years, including an extended 34-day evaluation with the 25th Infantry Division in 1983. Generally regarded as the first serious realworld test of the ration under actual field conditions, the MRE officially replaced the old CANC ration as the standard individual combat ration for American forces in the early 1980s. On paper, this looked like the finish line. It was not. The MRE's actual combat debut at scale came during Operation Desert Shield and Desert Storm in 1990 and 1991. And the reviews from the troops eating it were brutal. Soldiers with the kind of dark inventive humor that seems to follow every generation of military food started coming up with their own alternate meanings for the acronym MRE. Meals rejected by everyone. Meals refusing to exit. Worse variations circulated too, less printable ones. Part of the problem was logistical rather than culinary. Some of the MREs issued during the Gulf War had been sitting in pre-positioned war reserve stockpiles for four or 5 years or longer, cycling repeatedly through extreme desert heat that accelerated degradation of both flavor and nutritional quality well beyond what the rations were designed to withstand. But part of the problem really was the food itself. NADIC had, by its own later admission, approached menu design with what one longtime program director candidly called a father knows best mentality, loading the ration with traditional American comfort food that did not particularly resonate with the 18 to 24 year old troops, many from culturally distinct regional backgrounds, actually eating it in the desert. This decision to finally listen seriously to soldier feedback seemed small at the time. It was not. NATIC's combat feeding directorate spent the years following the Gulf War fundamentally overhauling the MRE program, expanding menu variety dramatically, adding ethnic and regional dishes, improving flavor science, and introducing genuinely useful new components. Since 1993, over 270 new food items have been added to the MRE rotation. In 1992, the military introduced the flameless ration heater, a small pouch containing a magnesium and iron alloy that when activated with a splash of water, triggers an exothermic chemical reaction, producing enough heat to warm an entree in the field without any open flame, any stove, or any electricity at all. Slide the entree pouch in, add water, fold it shut, and within about 10 to 12 minutes, a hot meal produced by nothing but a controlled chemical reaction happening in your hand. No fire, no fuel, no smoke to give away a position. That single innovation solved a problem that had existed since the Roman legions were forced to build fires just to eat. The modern MRE, as it exists today, is a genuinely impressive piece of engineering hiding inside deliberately unglamorous packaging. A standard case contains 12 different menus so that troops eating multiple meals a day for extended periods are not stuck facing total repetition. Each individual menu weighs around 1 and a2 pounds and typically delivers roughly 1,260 calories alongside a mix of entree, side, snack, beverage powder, and accessory items. Most sealed in that same flexible triaminate retort pouch technology first developed back in the 1970s. The Department of Defense requires every MRE to maintain a minimum shelf life of 3 years when stored at 80° Fahrenheit or below. And to accelerate testing for that requirement, NATIC places sample rations inside a 100 degree box for 6 months to simulate roughly 3 years of realworld aging in a fraction of the time. The packaging itself is durable enough to be safely air dropped by parachute from as high as 100 ft without rupturing. Meaning an MRE can quite literally be thrown out of the back of a moving aircraft and land ready to eat. But the MRE is far more than just food for soldiers marching through a desert. And this next part tends to catch people offguard even more than the space program connection did. The retort pouch and freeze drying technologies developed and refined at NATIC did not stay locked inside military supply chains. They spread almost immediately into the civilian world. The exact same preservation science powers the pouches of shelf stable tuna and chicken now sitting on ordinary grocery store shelves next to the canned versions. Lighter, faster to open, and often better tasting than their metal ancestors, it powers the backpacking and camping meal industry. Entire companies built around lightweight, just add water dinners for hikers who want a hot meal on a mountain side without carrying a cast iron pan. It powers disaster relief logistics worldwide where MRE style rations, sometimes literally military surplus MREs themselves, get distributed by the pallet after hurricanes, earthquakes, and floods. Precisely because they require no refrigeration, no cooking equipment, and no clean water beyond what is needed to activate a flameless heater. Somewhere between 6,000 and 600,000 [music] people from a stranded backpacker to an entire disaster zone have almost certainly eaten food descended directly from a laboratory in NICT Massachusetts without ever knowing it. Inside military circles, MREs have also become a strange sort of currency right down to individual components. Ask almost any American veteran and they will tell you without hesitation that the jalapeno cheese spread packet is the single most fought over, most heavily traded item to ever come out of an MRE case. Sometimes bartered for two or three other full entre at once. Certain unpopular entre, meanwhile, develop such lasting reputations for being inedible that soldiers gave them nicknames that outlived entire deployments. And NATIC's own food scientists have openly admitted in later interviews that soldier feedback data on which specific menus got quietly buried at the bottom of every case became one of their most useful research tools for deciding what to cut. This is the part that does not get enough credit. A sensory panel of trained tasters can rate a prototype meal all day long in a laboratory setting. But nothing tells the truth about a ration faster than watching what an actual 18-year-old private chooses to eat first and what gets left behind in the mud. Here is the genuinely startling modern fact. The kind that tends to stop people mid-sentence. The commercial military ration market, MREs, incomparable operational food systems supplied to armed forces around the world, is now estimated to be worth well over $1 billion annually on a global basis and continues climbing as more nations modernize their own field feeding programs using the same underlying retort pouch and flameless heating technology the United States pioneered decades ago. A problem that once killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers through nothing more sophisticated than spoiled meat and moldy biscuit has become a global billiondoll precision engineered industry complete with sensory testing panels that rate every prototype meal on a 9-point scale before it is ever allowed anywhere near an actual solders pack. It was there when Roman legions marched on roads built to feed them. It was there when sailors died by the tens of thousands from a vitamin deficiency nobody in charge wanted to pay to fix. It was there when Napoleon offered a king's ransom for a solution his own army would not live to benefit from. It was there when twothirds of America's Civil War debt fell not to bullets but to disease bred by contaminated rations. It was there when a Minnesota physiologist built a combat meal out of supermarket groceries to keep paratroopers alive over Normandy. It was there when engineers in a small Massachusetts lab handed the exact same packaging breakthrough to soldiers in the field and astronauts in orbit practically on the same afternoon. And it is there right now, sitting in a drawer in an emergency kit somewhere or tucked into a hiker's backpack or stacked by the pallet in a warehouse waiting for the next hurricane. A flat plastic pouch that can survive a 100 ft fall from an airplane, sit on a shelf for 3 years in the heat, and still turn into a hot meal in 10 minutes flat using nothing but a splash of water and a chemical reaction. Not bad, honestly, for a meal that soldiers spent decades calling meals rejected by everyone. If any part of this surprised you, the space food connection, the Civil War death toll, the fact that armies were still opening cans with hammers half a century after the can was invented, let me know in the comments which detail got you. Những người đầu tiên giải quyết vấn đề dinh dưỡng di động không phải là các nhà khoa học trong phòng thí nghiệm.
